views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep negotiating continuously with Lighthizer/Mnuchin and do not open a new tariff or hostage-style front while the List 3 hike is still suspended. Use additional agricultural and energy purchases as bargaining chips only against a written path to freeze or roll back U.S. Section 301 rates, and keep structural/IP language narrow enough that it does not lock in U.S. snapback rights or gut industrial-policy space. Hold the Meng/Huawei file on a separate legal-diplomatic track rather than trading it into an unfinished commercial deal.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is material but not existential. Combined U.S. Section 301 coverage is already ~$250B (List 1/2 at 25%, List 3 at 10% from 24 Sep 2018), and U.S. customs imports from China fell from $52.1B in Oct 2018 to $31.1B in Mar 2019 (−40%). Official factory PMI dropped to 49.2 in Feb with new export orders at 45.2, the weakest since 2009; Feb exports plunged 20.7% y/y (Jan–Feb still ~−5% after holiday smoothing), and 2018 GDP slowed to 6.6% with a 6.0–6.5% 2019 target. Huawei is under firm-level legal and 5G pressure (DOJ charges 28 Jan; Canada authorized Meng extradition proceedings 1 Mar). That cluster sits just below the +0.5 CHN anchor because there is no FX-reserve crisis in the available data, the Jan 1 / Mar 1 List 3 hike to 25% was delayed (24 Feb / 1 Mar), and talks are described as being in their “final weeks.” Escalation now would likely invite the postponed 25% hike and further export-hub job losses already visible in PMI employment. Maximal concession is also premature: Lighthizer told the Senate Finance Committee on 12 Mar that “major issues” (enforcement, IP/tech transfer, SOE subsidies, currency) remain open, China is pushing for full tariff removal, and the U.S. has not locked a matching rollback. Purchase talk has already featured in every 2019 round; converting that into a one-sided concede_purchases label without a reciprocal tariff path would spend leverage before the text is done. Negotiate — no new commitments beyond exploring a purchase-for-tariff-freeze package — is therefore the stance that matches a +0.42 threat reading.
key_factors: ~$250B of Chinese goods still under Section 301; List 3 10%→25% hike delayed but not cancelled
Sharp contraction in the U.S. China-import channel and Feb 2019 export/PMI slump
Huawei/Meng legal and 5G campaign is a separate firm-level and tech-sovereignty threat
Talks are live and in 'final weeks' but enforcement and structural issues remain unresolved
Unilateral escalation or one-sided purchase/structural giveaways would worsen, not hedge, the growth and legitimacy risk

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
G20 Buenos Aires dinner: 90-day negotiation window; planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended. Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
Trump tweets that talks have made substantial progress and further delays the scheduled List 3 hike from 10% to 25%.
Lighthizer and Mnuchin in Beijing for high-level talks. Purchase commitments discussed; enforcement and structural IP/tech-transfer issues unresolved.
U.S. imports of goods from China fell from 52081 (2018-10) to 31079 (2019-03), a ~40% decline over the window.
February exports fell 20.7 percent from a year earlier, the largest decline since February 2016; government targeting 6.0 to 6.5 percent growth in 2019 after 6.6 percent in 2018.
Official PMI fell to 49.2 in February; new export orders 45.2, lowest since February 2009; manufacturing output contracted for the first time since January 2009.

Lighthizer said major issues remain unresolved, hoped talks were in the 'final weeks,' and that China was pushing hard for all American tariffs to be removed while enforcement was still the biggest obstacle.
Meng extradition hearing opens in Vancouver during trade talks; Beijing sees the arrest as political and Huawei as a national champion under U.S. pressure.
